% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
Relation F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81], $p < 0.001$), attributable to grammar-layer elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions counted as false positives.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), lower than SciERC's 9.90\%.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR from 18.46\% to 26.17\% ($+$42\%).
This counter-intuitive result has a structural explanation: the unconstrained baseline's 29.66\% OOV relation triples cannot be evaluated for DR (no schema entry exists); grammar enforcement assigns these triples valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated entity types frequently violate.
The grammar layer thus \emph{reveals} latent type incompatibilities, directly motivating the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency and tightness ceiling.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by 25\% but fails to eliminate RV (29.87\%) and increases ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,4.22\%), replicating SciERC's pattern: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, semantic enforcement encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules, and the semantic mask occasionally forces OOV type alternatives.
Residual DR (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC's (0.93\%) due to higher constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$ vs.\ 0.333): the aggregate fallback rate (10.2\%; 1{,}770/17{,}341 triples) closely tracks residual DR, confirming a near-bijection between fallback events and violations.
Zero-shot R-F1 (6--8\%) serves as a control variable, not an optimization target (S2 omitted; residual is fallback-dominated, not coreference-driven).

\subsection{Cross-Task Validation: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

To test generality beyond RE, we apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 argument roles, 27 entity types, 245 role$\to$type constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}).
The constraint framework requires no architectural modification: the grammar layer compiles event/role vocabularies into a CFG; the semantic layer enforces role-conditioned entity type constraints via the same stateful registry mechanism.
The violation taxonomy extends naturally: Event Vocabulary (EV), Role Vocabulary (RoV), Argument Constraint (AC, analogous to DR), Entity Type (ET), and Cross-Field (CF).

\paragraph{Baselines and constrained results.}
Unconstrained generation produces extreme vocabulary violations across all three models (Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), far exceeding RE baselines (DocRED RV\,=\,29.7\%) because 80 argument roles exceed prompt-based reproduction capacity.
All models produce entity F1\,=\,0: violations are so severe (EV + RoV exceeding 85\% combined) that the parser fails to identify well-formed entity mentions.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all three models ($\to$\,0\%), confirming the tokenizer-agnostic claim across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
Residual AC under Full S1 ranges from 1.3\% (Mistral) to 3.8\% (Llama), driven by model confusion between semantically similar entity types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN, BOD vs.\ BAL) where grammar-first fallback permits the incorrect type.
CF rises to 15--21\%, consistent with the per-argument enforcement trade-off established in RE.

\paragraph{Layer ablation.}
Grammar-only configurations (Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}) isolate each layer's contribution.
Grammar eliminates EV entirely ($\to$\,0\%) but leaves RoV at high levels: 76.1\% (Qwen), 77.0\% (Llama), 64.0\% (Mistral), because the CFG enforces event type vocabulary but cannot constrain the combinatorial space of 80 argument roles conditioned on event context.
AC rises from near-zero to 8--14\% under grammar-only (Qwen 8.2\%, Llama 8.8\%, Mistral 13.8\%), replicating the latent-violation surfacing pattern from DocRED (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}): grammar forces valid role names, exposing underlying type incompatibilities.
Full S1 then drives RoV to 0\% across all models, confirming that the two layers are complementary: grammar guarantees structural well-formedness (EV\,$=$\,0), the semantic layer enforces ontological constraints (RoV\,$=$\,0).

\paragraph{Post-hoc filtering is impractical for EE.}
An alternative to constrained decoding is post-hoc filtering: discarding predictions that violate ontology constraints.
On WikiEvents, post-hoc filtering retains only 23 of 5{,}467 arguments for Qwen (99.6\% discarded), 3 of 5{,}053 for Llama (99.9\%), and 0 of 6{,}034 for Mistral (100\%).
The cause is systematic: unconstrained models generate generic role names (\textit{agent}, \textit{object}) rather than ontology-specific roles (\textit{Attacker}, \textit{Artifact}), producing outputs that are entirely off-schema.
This contrasts with RE, where post-hoc filtering is expensive but functional (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); in EE, it is not a viable alternative to constrained decoding.

\paragraph{Format compliance and extraction quality.}
Unlike RE, where constraints are F1-neutral ($<$1\,pp change), EE exhibits measurable performance gains under constrained decoding.
Entity F1 rises from 0\% to 11.7--17.6\% across all three models (Qwen 14.1\%, Llama 17.6\%, Mistral 11.7\%); Trigger F1 increases by $+$1.5 to $+$1.8\,pp.
The mechanism is format compliance, not improved semantic understanding: grammar enforcement produces schema-valid JSON that the parser can process, recovering entity mentions lost in off-schema output.
Trigger F1 gains trace to elimination of OOV event types counted as false positives.
This distinction matters for deployment: in pipelines requiring structured output, format enforcement delivers practical value beyond ontological correctness.

CF impact is model-dependent: for well-calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), S1 introduces CF violations (up to 12.02\%) as a consequence of per-relation independent enforcement; for poorly-calibrated models (Mistral), S1 substantially reduces CF (56.87\%\,$\to$\,1.27\%) by constraining type assignments to schema-valid values.

+CF fallback ablation shows that eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR ($+$13.85\,pp). CF$\leftrightarrow$DR thus represents a fundamental trade-off in composable constraint systems rather than an independently resolvable limitation (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}).
Entity F1 impact is model-dependent ($+$1.22\,pp for Qwen vs.\ $-$0.64\,pp for Llama on DocRED), partially confounded by increased parse failures under constraints (Llama: 9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%).
Zero-shot results cover three 7--8B-class models, where relation F1 remains around 4--8\% compared to $\sim$45\% for fine-tuned systems.

Composability with fine-tuned models is validated on both SciERC and DocRED with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\%, R-F1 change within $\pm$0.6\,pp), but evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); residual CF (Qwen 1.18\%, Llama 0.46\% on SciERC) traces to schema-level type ambiguity (\textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X) rather than enforcement failure.

(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.

-(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type---which may differ from the entity's registered type.

These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.

lines: \paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
\label{app:fallback-coverage}
The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.

-\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (36.6\% of type-bearing positions on SciERC) occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations---these events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.

+\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (36.6\% of type-bearing positions on SciERC) occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations. These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.

Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.

\section{Reproducibility Details}
\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).
SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.

\paragraph{Inference time.}
Table~\ref{tab:inference-time} reports per-document inference times for Qwen3-8B under zero-shot greedy decoding across constraint configurations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Inference time (seconds/document, mean $\pm$ std) for Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:inference-time}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{SciERC} & \textbf{DocRED} \\
\midrule
Unconstrained       & $8.69 \pm 3.89$  & $19.75 \pm 8.99$  \\
Grammar-only        & $8.81 \pm 4.51$  & $20.58 \pm 10.75$ \\
Semantic-only       & $7.23 \pm 3.91$  & $20.53 \pm 9.37$  \\
Full S1             & $6.76 \pm 3.67$  & $20.39 \pm 9.43$  \\
Post-hoc            & $8.69 \pm 3.89$  & $19.78 \pm 8.99$  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On SciERC, full S1 constrained decoding is 22\% \emph{faster} than unconstrained generation because suppressing invalid tokens reduces output length.
On DocRED (longer documents), the masking computation adds a small constant overhead (+3.2\%) that slightly exceeds the token-savings effect.
Grammar-only and post-hoc filtering add negligible overhead ($<$4.2\% and $<$0.2\%, respectively).

\subsection{SciERC Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC,
evaluating each constraint layer independently and in combination.
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 551 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters;
only the active constraint layers differ.

%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────

\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
DR: domain/range violation rate;
RV: relation vocabulary violation rate;
ET: entity type violation rate;
CF: cross-field consistency violation rate.
$\Delta$DR: relative DR reduction vs.\ the unconstrained baseline.
$\downarrow$\,/\,$\uparrow$: lower\,/\,higher is better.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded; see text).
F1 scores are multiplied by 100.

\label{tab:scierc-ablation}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
At the per-relation level, violations drop from 42.42\% to 2.82\% on
\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004
The residual ET under semantic-only arises because the semantic mask constrains type tokens to relation-specific valid sets but cannot enforce vocabulary membership; occasionally the mask excludes the model's preferred valid-vocabulary type, forcing an OOV alternative.
Under full mode, the grammar layer's intersection prevents this, confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV relation types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% relative reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} presents the composability matrix on SciERC for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (zero-shot vs.\ LoRA fine-tuned $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ full S1), testing whether OntoCoDec composes with task-specific fine-tuning across model families.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
The four-way ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) shows grammar is a no-op post-fine-tuning; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\%.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned) for Qwen, tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) offers an orthogonal path: on SciERC, it eliminates residual DR entirely and reduces CF from 9.90\% to 0.53\% for Qwen, and from 6.56\% to 0.93\% for Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
Relation F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81], $p < 0.001$), attributable to grammar-layer elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions counted as false positives.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), lower than SciERC's 9.90\%.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR from 18.46\% to 26.17\% ($+$42\%).
This counter-intuitive result has a structural explanation: the unconstrained baseline's 29.66\% OOV relation triples cannot be evaluated for DR (no schema entry exists); grammar enforcement assigns these triples valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated entity types frequently violate.
The grammar layer thus \emph{reveals} latent type incompatibilities, directly motivating the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency and tightness ceiling.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by 25\% but fails to eliminate RV (29.87\%) and increases ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,4.22\%), replicating SciERC's pattern: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, semantic enforcement encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules, and the semantic mask occasionally forces OOV type alternatives.
Residual DR (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC's (0.93\%) due to higher constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$ vs.\ 0.333): the aggregate fallback rate (10.2\%; 1{,}770/17{,}341 triples) closely tracks residual DR, consistent with a near-bijection between fallback events and violations.
Zero-shot R-F1 (6--8\%) serves as a control variable, not an optimization target (S2 omitted; residual is fallback-dominated, not coreference-driven).

CF impact is model-dependent: for well-calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), S1 introduces CF violations (up to 12.02\%) as a consequence of per-relation independent enforcement; for poorly-calibrated models (Mistral), S1 substantially reduces CF (56.87\%\,$\to$\,1.27\%) by constraining type assignments to schema-valid values.
CF fallback ablation shows that eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR ($+$13.85\,pp). CF$\leftrightarrow$DR thus represents a fundamental trade-off in composable constraint systems rather than an independently resolvable limitation (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}).
Entity F1 impact is model-dependent ($+$1.22\,pp for Qwen vs.\ $-$0.64\,pp for Llama on DocRED), partially confounded by increased parse failures under constraints (Llama: 9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%).
Zero-shot results cover three 7--8B-class models, where relation F1 remains around 4--8\% compared to $\sim$45\% for fine-tuned systems.
Composability with fine-tuned models is validated on both SciERC and DocRED with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\%, R-F1 change within $\pm$0.6\,pp), but evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); residual CF (Qwen 1.18\%, Llama 0.46\% on SciERC) traces to schema-level type ambiguity (\textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X) rather than enforcement failure.
The semantic layer's dynamic masking assumes each entity type maps to a unique first subword token, verified for both tokenizers on our two ontologies (6 entity types each), but ontologies with many types or multi-token type names would require prefix-tree masking, which we have not implemented.
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF violations.
All models tested are 7--8B-parameter class; scaling behavior to larger (70B+) or smaller models has not been verified, and the dual-factor pattern's predictive scope may differ at other scales.
CF type inconsistencies may propagate to downstream tasks that consume extracted triples (e.g., knowledge graph construction, question answering); the impact of such propagation has not been evaluated.
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations across all fine-tuned settings, both models and both datasets) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors correctly caught by constraints (28\%); Llama DocRED alone accounts for 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), reflecting weaker entity typing (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
Schema coverage gaps (one-third of residual violations) are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone (training-set frequency coverage); complementary approaches such as global type consensus or post-hoc correction may address this limitation.
All main experiments use greedy decoding; our evaluation of beam search on the full SciERC test set (551 documents) and a DocRED subset across three models confirms compatibility (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}), but comprehensive evaluation across all decoding configurations remains future work.

%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
At the per-relation level, violations drop from 42.42\% to 2.82\% on
\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004
The residual ET under semantic-only arises because the semantic mask constrains type tokens to relation-specific valid sets but cannot enforce vocabulary membership; occasionally the mask excludes the model's preferred valid-vocabulary type, forcing an OOV alternative.
Under full mode, the grammar layer's intersection prevents this, confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV relation types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% relative reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} presents the composability matrix on SciERC for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (zero-shot vs.\ LoRA fine-tuned $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ full S1), testing whether OntoCoDec composes with task-specific fine-tuning across model families.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
The four-way ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) shows grammar is a no-op post-fine-tuning; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\%.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned) for Qwen, tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) offers an orthogonal path: on SciERC, it eliminates residual DR entirely and reduces CF from 9.90\% to 0.53\% for Qwen, and from 6.56\% to 0.93\% for Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters grammar$\cap$semantic$=$\emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters grammar$\cap$semantic$=$\emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
This confirms that the three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Wall-clock overhead is modest; \texttt{early\_stopping} terminates generation once all beams produce a complete sequence, limiting the additional compute to partial-sequence exploration rather than full-length replication.

With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).

lines: We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
Within this design, the current full S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.

-The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are inversely associated (Spearman $\rho = -0.77$, $n{=}6$), with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:main-results}).

+The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are inversely associated (Spearman $\rho = -0.77$, $n{=}6$), with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}).

The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.

While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.

The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-search}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 1.58 & 6.85 & 55.35 & 6.12 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:beam-ablation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
This confirms that the three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Wall-clock overhead is modest; \texttt{early\_stopping} terminates generation once all beams produce a complete sequence, limiting the additional compute to partial-sequence exploration rather than full-length replication.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

\subsection{Ablation and Composability with Fine-Tuning}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC,
evaluating each constraint layer independently and in combination.
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 551 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters;
only the active constraint layers differ.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}

  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\

\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
DR: domain/range violation rate;
RV: relation vocabulary violation rate;
ET: entity type violation rate;

$\downarrow$\,/\,$\uparrow$: lower\,/\,higher is better.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded; see text).
F1 scores are multiplied by 100.

\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains from aggressive violation removal (SciERC: 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED: 9.61 vs.\ 8.23), but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}); OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation.
At the per-relation level, violations drop from 42.42\% to 2.82\% on
\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and ET (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%) with no F1 impact, while DR remains unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%).
This configuration represents the capability ceiling of grammar-based constrained decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}, which enforces JSON structure and vocabulary membership but cannot reason about cross-field semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and cannot eliminate RV (1.51\%) or ET (0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004
The residual ET under semantic-only arises because the semantic mask constrains type tokens to relation-specific valid sets but cannot enforce vocabulary membership; occasionally the mask excludes the model's preferred valid-vocabulary type, forcing an OOV alternative.
Under full mode, the grammar layer's intersection prevents this, confirming the \emph{enabling dependency}: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV relation types with no domain/range rules.
Adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% relative reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, CF=0.0803, triples=1644

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning
%  exp_ids: lora_scierc_unconstrained, lora_scierc_full_s1
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Table~\ref{tab:composability} presents the composability matrix on SciERC for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (zero-shot vs.\ LoRA fine-tuned $\times$ unconstrained vs.\ full S1), testing whether OntoCoDec composes with task-specific fine-tuning across model families.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Adding S1 eliminates these: Qwen DR 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\% ($-$0.09\,pp R-F1), Llama DR 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\% ($+$0.02\,pp).
On DocRED, the same pattern holds: Qwen DR 0.76\%\,$\to$\,0.01\% ($-$0.30\,pp), Llama DR 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0.20\% ($+$0.51\,pp).
% w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.01%, R-F1=40.56; w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval: DR=0.20%, R-F1=44.23

Across all settings, fine-tuned + S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
The four-way ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}) shows grammar is a no-op post-fine-tuning; the semantic layer alone reduces DR by 39--72\%.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned) for Qwen, tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) offers an orthogonal path: on SciERC, it eliminates residual DR entirely and reduces CF from 9.90\% to 0.53\% for Qwen, and from 6.56\% to 0.93\% for Llama (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation} presents the four-way ablation on DocRED, a document-level RE benchmark with 96 Wikidata relation types (14$\times$ the ontology size of SciERC).
All experiments use Qwen3-8B zero-shot on 998 documents.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: DocRED four-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}

  & \textbf{0.03} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.07

  & 29.87 & 4.22
  & 1.05
  & 7.70  & 57.81 \\

\label{tab:docred-ablation}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%; residual traces to tokenization edge cases where multi-token relation names span grammar-state boundaries).
Relation F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81], $p < 0.001$), attributable to grammar-layer elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions counted as false positives.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), lower than SciERC's 9.90\%, consistent with the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off analyzed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR from 18.46\% to 26.17\% ($+$42\%).
This counter-intuitive result has a structural explanation: the unconstrained baseline's 29.66\% OOV relation triples cannot be evaluated for DR (no schema entry exists); grammar enforcement assigns these triples valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated entity types frequently violate.
The grammar layer thus \emph{reveals} latent type incompatibilities, directly motivating the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency and tightness ceiling.}
Semantic-only reduces DR by 25\% but fails to eliminate RV (29.87\%) and increases ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,4.22\%), replicating SciERC's pattern: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, semantic enforcement encounters OOV types with no domain/range rules, and the semantic mask occasionally forces OOV type alternatives.
Residual DR (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC's (0.93\%) due to higher constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$ vs.\ 0.333): the grammar-first fallback rate reaches 10.2\% (1{,}770/17{,}341 triples), yielding an effective semantic constraint coverage of 89.8\% (vs.\ 63.4\% on SciERC for Llama; Appendix~\ref{app:fallback-coverage}). The fallback rate closely tracks residual DR, consistent with a near-bijection between fallback events and violations.
Zero-shot R-F1 (6--8\%) serves as a control variable, not an optimization target (S2 omitted; residual is fallback-dominated, not coreference-driven).
